Background: Providing a Shared Understanding
• The pandemic has complicated state assessment in unforeseen
ways.
• As states move forward with testing, being clear about the
purposes of analyses will be more important than ever
▪ Time is short and the context is fraught
▪ Assessment is often confounded with accountability
▪ Planning of school supports should go hand in hand with plans for
analysis

Key Questions of Interest
• Who participated in the test in 2021?
• What do the test scores mean in 2021?
• Are the individual and aggregate scores in 2021 comparable to those in
previous years?
• What are appropriate (or inappropriate) uses of test scores in 2021?
• Which schools and districts have the largest decreases in performance?
▪ What characteristics explain, or at least associate with, these decreases?
• What subgroups display the largest decreases?
• Do students in remote learning conditions perform differently than those in
in-person learning conditions?
• Etc.
www.nciea.org

Operational Analyses
• Sound investigative analyses are predicated upon assessment data
of high technical quality.
▪ Operational analyses tend to proceed investigative analyses
▪ Sound investigative analyses can occur with compromised assessment data,
but such cases are rare (e.g., getting to the right conclusion with the wrong
data)

• Concerns about validity of the data derived from assessments
abound, e.g.,
▪ Comparability of remote versus in-person testing
▪ Impact of low participation rates (e.g., potential impacts on item
parameters under post equating, possible impacts on normative statistics)
www.nciea.org

Investigative analyses
• Assuming assessment data of
good technical quality, what
investigative analyses should be
pursued?
• USED’s recent relaxation of
accountability provisions makes
investigative analyses even more
critical.
• Typical analyses that support
accountability are not the only, or
even the major, stories we want
to investigate this year.
www.nciea.org

Investigative analyses
• Support planning/intervention is rooted in our ideas, or
hypothesis, about what we think is happening to students
▪ Based on our current, incomplete picture of student experiences
• These hypotheses should be tested and the results used to
inform and revise our support plans
▪ Support plans should be ready to run with the results of planned
analyses (and in worse case scenarios, run without the data
anyway)
▪ Support plans should be amenable to change as new data/
evidence becomes available.

Some Overarching Questions
• How did overall performance change relative to prior years?
• Who has the lowest performance?
• How does performance compare across key groups?

www.nciea.org

Using Investigative Analyses to Support Planning
• Hypothesis: The academic impact (sometimes referred to as
learning loss) of the pandemic is being unevenly felt by
students.
• If true, targeted intervention is more prudent than blanket
intervention.
• For states considering targeted assistance:
▪ Who needs help? Grades, schools, districts, demographic subgroups,
COVID related subgroups, English Language Learners.
▪ What do they need help in? Mathematics, ELA, Science, non-tested
subjects?
▪ How much help do they need? Is recovery needed large or small?
www.nciea.org

Many Factors to Consider
• Unit. At what level will the analyses be focused?
▪ Individual students
▪ Classrooms, schools, districts, or the state overall
▪ Specific subgroups (e.g., race/ethnicity, economically disadvantaged,
students with disabilities, English language learners)
▪ Specific grades (and grade-groupings, like early elementary) or content areas
▪ Learning conditions (e.g. remote, in-person, hybrid)
• Measure. What outcome measure will be examined?
▪ Achievement (e.g., level scale scores or proficiency levels), often in terms of
cross-sectional comparisons
▪ Growth (e.g., score differences on a vertical scale, student growth
percentiles), often in terms of longitudinal comparisons
▪ Gaps between groups defined in terms of achievement or growth

www.nciea.org

Prioritizing Analyses
• Internal vs. External
▪ Are the results are intended for use outside of department, and if
so, what specific stakeholders are meant to be addressed?
• Availability
▪ How easily accessible will the data be?
▪ Like the distinction of internal vs. external, level of access involves
stakeholders and refers to the specific ways in which the results will
be provided and communicated (e.g., posted on the department
website, communicated through a press release, as part of a
webinar).

www.nciea.org

Prioritizing Analyses
• Reporting Format
▪ How will the results be provided (e.g., a simple spreadsheet, posted as part
of the state’s report card, as an interactive web-based visualization)?
• Timing
▪ Is there a specific window of time by which the results are needed? For
example, is there a window of time an analysis needs to be completed by
to support an intervention?
▪ Results will likely come in waves from different data sources, how will this
impact timing.
• Responsible Party
▪ Who will be conducting the analyses and what is their capacity to
implement the analyses? Will the analysis be seen as credible to key
stakeholders when coming from that responsible party?

www.nciea.org

Example Investigative analyses for 2021
Participation
• Participation rates on assessments are likely to be
substantially less than in normal years.
• Understanding who and who did not participate in state
assessments will be critical in interpreting overall results.
▪ By demographic subgroups (e.g., ses, ethnicity)
▪ By mode of instruction (remote/hybrid/in person learner)
▪ By grade, school, district

www.nciea.org

Example Investigative analyses for 2021:
Using Growth to Assesses Impact
• Student academic growth analyses can be used to assess the
academic impact of the pandemic.
• Baseline skip-year growth norms (2017 to 2019) can be used
with 2019 to 2021 data to assess how much “slower”
students learned during the pandemic relative to pre-
pandemic times.
• Differential impact on groups can be investigated by
aggregating up SGPs at the group level.
• With accurate mode of instruction data (remote/hybrid/in
person), impact of mode of instruction can be assessed.
